title: Maintain Safety and Health Standards in a Grain Handling and Storage Environment

lessons.title: Hazards in grain handling and storage
lessons.html:
A high-risk workplace

Grain depots look peaceful outside the harvest rush, but they contain some of the most serious hazards in agriculture. The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires the employer to provide and maintain a safe workplace, identify hazards, assess risks and apply controls, and train and supervise workers. The depot manager is responsible for making this happen on site.

Major hazards

HazardWherePossible harm
EngulfmentBins, silos, bunkers, trucksSuffocation in flowing or bridged grain
Dust explosion and fireElevators, tunnels, dryers, filtersMultiple deaths, destruction of structures
Toxic gasesFumigated structures, confined spacesPhosphine poisoning, oxygen deficiency
EntanglementConveyors, augers, elevator boots, drivesAmputation, death
FallsSilo tops, ladders, truck tops, gantriesSerious injury, death
VehiclesYard, weighbridge, tipping areasCrushing, collisions
Dust and noiseIntake, cleaning, elevatorsLung disease, hearing loss
Heat and fatigueLong harvest shiftsHeat stress, errors

Risk assessment

  1. List all tasks, including non-routine ones such as bin cleaning, unblocking and maintenance.
  2. Identify hazards and who could be harmed.
  3. Rate risk by likelihood and consequence.
  4. Apply the hierarchy of controls: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, PPE.
  5. Communicate the assessment to workers and review it after incidents and changes.

Involve health and safety representatives and the health and safety committee, as the OHS Act provides for, in inspections and in reviewing risk assessments.

Remember that non-routine tasks, such as cleaning out a bin at the end of the season or clearing a blocked elevator boot, are where many serious grain incidents happen. These tasks need specific risk assessments and close supervision every time.

lessons.title: Controls, permits and emergency response
lessons.html:
Key controls

  • Lock-out / tag-out – isolate, lock, tag and test before any work on equipment; each worker places their own lock.
  • Bin entry permits – avoid entry where possible; when unavoidable require isolation of all equipment, atmosphere testing, harness and lifeline, trained standby, and rescue plan. Never enter while grain is flowing or when grain is bridged above.
  • Hot work permits – remove dust, fire watch, extinguishers, gas test where needed.
  • Working at height – guardrails, fall arrest equipment, trained workers.
  • Fumigation control – only trained, registered fumigators; placards, gas monitoring, exclusion zones and clearance before re-entry.
  • Dust control – extraction, housekeeping schedules, magnets, elevator monitoring, suitable electrical equipment.
  • Traffic management – one-way routes, speed limits, pedestrian walkways, banksmen at tipping.
  • PPE – respirators suited to the dust, hearing protection, safety boots, reflective vests, harnesses.
  • Health – medical surveillance for dust and noise exposure where required, hydration and rest breaks.

Training and supervision

Induct all staff, seasonal workers and contractors. Train and authorise people for high-risk tasks. Supervisors must check that procedures are followed and stop unsafe work.

Emergency preparedness

  • Written emergency plans for engulfment, fire or explosion, gas exposure, injuries and severe weather.
  • Trained rescue team or arrangements with emergency services, and rescue equipment at the site.
  • Trained first aiders and stocked first aid boxes. First aid skills must be learnt through hands-on training with an accredited provider.
  • Regular drills and checks of alarms, escape routes and fire equipment.

In an engulfment, never send untrained people into the bin; shut down all grain flow, raise the alarm and follow the rescue plan. Many grain deaths are would-be rescuers.

Incidents

Report and investigate all incidents and near misses for root causes, report incidents to the Department of Employment and Labour where the OHS Act requires, and track actions to closure.

Key points

  • Engulfment, dust explosions, toxic gases, entanglement, falls and vehicles are major depot hazards.
  • Assess risks for all tasks, including non-routine ones, and apply the hierarchy of controls.
  • Use lock-out, bin entry, hot work and fumigation controls without exception.
  • Train, supervise and prepare for emergencies with drills and rescue plans.
  • Never send untrained people into a bin; stop grain flow, raise the alarm and follow the plan.
